strengths: Proposes SUIT, a subspace-aware locate-then-edit method that constrains edits to critical key and residual subspaces, yielding a clear and practical contribution to knowledge editing.

Extensive evaluation on three LLMs (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B), two benchmarks (CounterFact and zsRE), and strong baselines including AlphaEdit, MEMIT, PMET, MEND, and FT-L, with additional baselines in the appendix.

Demonstrates large specificity gains over strong baselines, e.g., +43.2 points over AlphaEdit on LLaMA-3-8B CounterFact, while maintaining high efficacy, generalization, fluency, consistency, and general capability in most settings.

Includes substantial analysis: perturbation heatmaps, variance decomposition of key subspaces, measurement of update leakage into the entity-agnostic subspace, steering effects of w1/w2, hyperparameter tradeoff analysis, and ablation of the key and residual components.
Reports both generation-based and probability-based metrics, evaluates sequential editing at 1000 and 5000 edits, and provides general capability results across six benchmarks.
The paper is generally well organized, with detailed appendices covering experimental setup, hyperparameters, and additional results; code and data are promised for release.
weaknesses: The key subspace identification applies SVD to uncentered key vectors and removes top principal directions as an 'entity-agnostic' subspace. Because uncentered SVD can be dominated by the mean/common bias, the theoretical link to low-variance entity-agnostic features is not fully rigorous; centering or an explicit variance-based criterion would better support the stated hypothesis.

The same global subspace is removed for all subjects and edits, and it is unclear how this subspace behaves across different relations and whether it may inadvertently remove relation-specific information. The procedure for computing ParaRel subject key vectors (which prompts/relations are used) is not sufficiently detailed for full reproducibility.

The residual vector is restricted to a 2D subspace with an orthogonality penalty, but the optimization and additive swap ignore interactions between w1 and w2. The paper notes that the directions are not fully disentangled (w1 also suppresses the old object, w2 also promotes the new object), so a more principled guarantee or derivation would strengthen the method.

The general capability evaluation for Qwen2.5 reports very low MMLU F1 scores (e.g., 2.46 pre-edit), raising concerns about the reliability of that benchmark/metric for some models. There are also small inconsistencies in GC scores between Table 1 and Appendix Table 6.
Computational cost and runtime are not reported, despite per-edit optimization of w1/w2 and SVD preprocessing over 10,000 subjects. Efficiency relative to baselines such as AlphaEdit is unclear.

Notation is occasionally inconsistent (e.g., K_s^⊥ vs. a global subspace, residual vector δ vs. δ', r vs. δ), and there are minor typos. These do not undermine the core results but slightly reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important and active problem: preserving unrelated knowledge during locate-then-edit knowledge editing.
Clear high-level motivation from the Linear Representation Hypothesis and a plausible two-part strategy: constrain the key vector and constrain the residual update.
Experiments cover three LLMs (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two standard editing benchmarks (CounterFact, zsRE), including sequential editing and general-capability evaluation.
Reports substantial improvements on several metrics, especially generation-based specificity on CounterFact, and provides ablations for the key-space and residual-space components.
Includes some useful analyses: perturbation heatmaps, hyperparameter tradeoff plots, and component-effect visualizations.
weaknesses: The central subspace-identification method is not convincingly validated. Removing top PCA directions from a global key matrix is assumed to yield an entity-agnostic subspace, but no evidence shows these directions correspond to semantic common features rather than high-variance entity-specific information. The validation in Table 2 is largely circular, and Table 3 is nearly tautological because the projected key construction forces near-orthogonality to the removed subspace.

The residual vector construction and its integration with the AlphaEdit update are insufficiently specified. It is unclear how the 2D residual update δ′ is converted into per-layer residuals r, whether prior keys K_p and projection P are recomputed with projected keys, and how these choices affect sequential editing.

The headline specificity gains rely on a generation-based criterion that is non-standard for specificity in this literature. The probability-based results in Appendix F.2 show much smaller gains (e.g., LLaMA AlphaEdit 72.7 vs. SUIT 84.4 specificity), which weakens the claimed dramatic improvement.

The analyses are less informative than they appear: δ∥W is expected to be more effective because w1 and w2 are optimized to increase o*; the variance comparison is constructed after removing components; and the paper itself admits w1/w2 are not fully disentangled, undermining the clean swap motivation.

Evaluation lacks statistical significance tests, runtime/memory comparisons, and strong simple baselines such as direct projection/erasure methods. Some reported general-capability changes are anomalous (e.g., Qwen average GC improves after 1000 edits), suggesting metric noise or sensitivity.

Reproducibility and presentation quality are poor. The code/data are not released, many method details are deferred or unclear, and the references are badly mangled with inconsistent citation labels and corrupted entries.

The method is somewhat incremental: it combines PCA-based key projection with a constrained residual edit and AlphaEdit-style closed-form update, but does not provide strong theoretical or empirical evidence that this specific decomposition is more principled than existing null-space or regularization approaches.
Ethical implications of making knowledge editing more efficient/precise are not discussed, despite the potential for misuse in altering factual model behavior.

strengths: The paper proposes SUIT, a novel subspace-aware knowledge editing method that constrains both the key vector and residual vector to edit-relevant subspaces, yielding strong specificity improvements over strong baselines such as AlphaEdit and MEMIT.

The empirical results are convincing: SUIT achieves large gains in specificity on COUNTERFACT (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B over AlphaEdit) while maintaining high efficacy and generalization, and it also performs well on ZSRE and in 5,000-edit sequential settings.

The evaluation is broad and rigorous, covering three models, two standard datasets, multiple metrics (efficacy, generalization, specificity, fluency, consistency, general capability), and additional baselines in the appendix.

The analyses are thorough and well-motivated: perturbation reduction at the subject's last token, subspace variance and update-effect analyses, steering experiments for w1/w2, hyperparameter tradeoff analysis, and component ablation studies.

The method is simple and modular, building on the locate-then-edit paradigm with a clear closed-form update and practical hyperparameters, and the paper promises code/data release for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: SUIT extends existing locate-then-edit methods (especially AlphaEdit) with subspace constraints, and the core update formula is adapted from prior work.

Some technical details are underspecified, such as whether the SVD for the key subspace is applied to centered or uncentered key vectors, how K_p is handled in the SUIT update, and the exact computational cost of optimizing w1 and w2 per edit.

The residual vector construction assumes w1 and w2 are orthogonal and have fully disentangled roles, but the paper itself shows they are not fully disentangled; this may limit the theoretical cleanliness of the approach and leaves room for future work.

The method introduces several hyperparameters (tau_energy, lambda) and uses fixed values across models; while a tradeoff analysis is provided, sensitivity and robustness across more diverse edit distributions are not fully established.

The general capability results, while competitive, are not uniformly better than the pre-edit model or AlphaEdit across all models, and the paper relies mostly on COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, which may not capture all real-world editing scenarios.

strengths: Novel subspace-aware knowledge editing method that grounds the locate-then-edit paradigm in the Linear Representation Hypothesis by constraining both the key vector and the residual vector to edit-relevant subspaces.

Substantial empirical gains in specificity over strong baselines such as AlphaEdit and MEMIT, e.g., +43.2 specificity points on LLaMA-3-8B COUNTERFACT, while maintaining high efficacy and general capability.

Comprehensive experimental validation across three models (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks (COUNTERFACT, ZSRE), with additional analyses on perturbation reduction, subspace variance, update leakage, w1/w2 roles, hyperparameter trade-offs, and ablations.

Demonstrates robustness in sequential editing (5,000 edits), context-robust editing (CHED), larger-model scaling (LLaMA2-13B), and RippleEdits, indicating practical applicability beyond standard metrics.
Reasonable pre-computation cost analysis and evidence that the chosen 10,000-subject subspace is close to the full-data subspace, supporting practical deployment.
weaknesses: Theoretical justification for the subspace decomposition is incomplete: the method assumes top singular vectors of the subject key matrix represent an entity-agnostic subspace, but this may conflate other shared or relation-level structure. The energy threshold tau_energy is empirically chosen rather than derived.

The residual-vector update is restricted to a 2D subspace via learned directions w1 and w2, but the additive swap relies on an orthogonality assumption that is only softly encouraged by a penalty. The authors acknowledge that w1 and w2 are not fully disentangled, which weakens the claimed precision of the subspace edit.

There is a factual inconsistency in the text: the paper claims 'highest Specificity on Qwen (96.6%)' for ZSRE, but Table 1 reports 81.7 and the probability-based table reports 95.0. This reduces confidence in the precision of the reported results.
Evaluation is limited to factual knowledge editing on standard datasets; generalization to other knowledge types, relations, languages, or editing scenarios is not fully explored.

Although baselines are run with unified hyperparameters following prior work, some weaker baselines (e.g., MEND) may be disadvantaged by tuning choices. Reproducibility depends on code and data promised but not yet released.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving specificity in locate-then-edit knowledge editing while maintaining high efficacy.
Proposes a clear and simple method (SUIT) that combines subspace projection for key vectors and a low-rank residual update.
Provides extensive experiments across three LLMs and two standard datasets, with many baselines and additional analyses (perturbation, subspace validation, hyperparameter, ablation, scaling).
Reports substantial empirical gains, especially in specificity and overall S score, over strong baselines such as AlphaEdit.
Includes practical considerations like pre-computation cost and subspace similarity for different N, and promises code release.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely combines existing ideas—null-space projection, SVD-based subspace removal, and low-rank residual edits—into a heuristic pipeline without a fundamentally new insight.

The theoretical justification for treating top principal components of subject key vectors from ParaRel as an 'entity-agnostic' subspace is questionable; high-variance directions across subjects more likely encode entity-specific variation, making the central hypothesis under-supported.

The ZSRE evaluation uses a non-standard specificity metric (model's own previous outputs) and omits the standard pre-knowledge check, which weakens comparability to prior work and may inflate reported specificity.

Important implementation details for the 2D residual subspace optimization (w1, w2) are missing, including initialization, learning rate, number of steps, and per-edit runtime, hindering reproducibility.

The very large gains over AlphaEdit (e.g., +43.2 specificity on LLaMA COUNTERFACT) are surprising and would require independent verification; potential hyperparameter or implementation unfairness is not ruled out.
The paper contains numerous typographical and citation errors (wrong years, author mismatches, inconsistent references), indicating insufficient care in preparation.
No limitations or ethical considerations are discussed, which is important for knowledge-editing methods that could be misused to inject false information.

strengths: Introduces a novel subspace-aware approach to locate-then-edit knowledge editing, constraining both key and residual updates to edit-relevant subspaces.
Achieves large empirical gains in specificity over strong baselines (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B COUNTERFACT) while maintaining high efficacy and generalization.
Extensive evaluation across three model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks, plus additional 5,000-edit, CHED, RippleEdits, and LLaMA2-13B experiments.
Provides detailed analyses validating the hypothesized roles of the entity-agnostic subspace and the two-dimensional residual subspace, including variance, projection, and steering experiments.
Includes ablation and hyperparameter tradeoff studies, showing synergy between key and residual components and reasonable robustness to hyperparameter choices.
Clear writing and organization, with a well-motivated method grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
weaknesses: The method is largely a combination of existing ideas (SVD-based subspace removal and low-rank residual updates) within the AlphaEdit framework; novelty is moderate compared to a fundamentally new editing paradigm.

The ZSRE specificity metric is changed from standard ground-truth token-level partial credit to a model-generated reference, which complicates direct comparison with prior work; a stricter standard evaluation is only provided in the appendix.

The residual vector update assumes a two-dimensional subspace and swaps projections, but the two directions are not fully disentangled, as acknowledged, raising questions about theoretical cleanliness.

Some design choices (e.g., removing top principal components of key vectors across many subjects/relations) are heuristic and could discard relation- or context-specific information, though empirical results are strong.
Reproducibility is limited by the absence of source code and data at review time, though the authors promise release upon publication.
General Capability still degrades on some models (e.g., GPT-J) relative to pre-edit performance, although it is better than AlphaEdit.
